cards.def: The belief that kings get their power from God, not the people, which the 1649 execution of Charles I overturned.
England's state governed without a monarch, ruled by Oliver Cromwell after 1649.
The period after 1660 when the monarchy, court, Church of England, and professional theater were restored under Charles II.
The doctrine, named for Dutch theologian Arminius and advanced by Laud, that God made redemption freely available to all.
The Puritan belief that God decided in advance who would be saved or damned, Christ's sacrifice being only for the "elect."
The older model in which the earth is fixed and the other heavenly bodies orbit it.
Fire, earth, water, and air, once thought to make up all matter.
The ordered ranking of creation from God, angels, humans, animals, plants to rocks, mirrored in the state from king to laborers.
London's law schools, one of the small centers of the literary reading public.
Young poets mentored by Ben Jonson, including Carew, Lovelace, Suckling, Waller, Vaughan, and Herrick.
Donne's school of poetry marked by learned terms and unusual analogies, a term coined by Samuel Johnson.
A royalist writer or poet who supported the king during the civil wars.
A court entertainment that under Charles I celebrated chivalric virtue and divine love symbolized by the royal marriage.
The Parliament convened in 1640 that refused to disband, abolished extralegal taxes, and executed Laud and Strafford.
The part of the Commons left after Cromwell's New Model Army expelled royalists and Presbyterians, which tried and executed Charles I.
Historians who think short-term causes like luck, personality, and bad decisions caused the civil wars.
Weekly news pamphlets that flourished in the 1640s when Parliament disrupted press censorship.
